info.title: khf-t-api-v1
info.description:
khf-t-api-v1 provides authenticated endpoints for the skills / curriculum domain, including multilingual translations, full-text and semantic search, and file operations.

API docs default style : docs

API docs scalar style : scalar

post.description: Returns a JWT access token for the given username and password.

parameters.name: type

schema.title: Token type
schema.description: Channel the token is being issued for, written to `usr_tokens.type`. Defaults to `ui`, the browser front end that posts this form; a script or an integration asks for `api` so its tokens can be told apart from interface logins when they are listed or revoked. A query parameter rather than a form field, so the request body stays exactly the OAuth2 password grant every client already knows how to send. A label on the row and nothing more - what a token may do is decided by the account's `token_scope_*` columns alone, so naming another type widens nothing.

post.description: Reports whether the given username and password are a valid, enabled login, and for a valid one the `usr_users.ui_level` of the account. No token is issued and no session is started. A correct password on a disabled account is reported as invalid, matching what `/auth/token` would do with the same credentials. Wrong credentials are answered 200 with `valid: false`; the one error case is a correct credential pair on an account whose `usr_users.require_password_change` is set, which is refused with 403 so the caller sends the user to change their password instead of on into the interface.

200.description: A JSON object whose `valid` field is true only for correct credentials, and whose `ui_level` field is `none` unless it is.

post.summary: [pending] Change the password of the calling user
post.description:
**Required scope:** `pending`

Replaces the password of the account the bearer token belongs to. The current password must be supplied and is verified again, so a stolen token on its own cannot be used to take an account over. Any bearer token of an enabled user is accepted, whatever its scopes, since changing one's own password is not a privileged action. A successful change clears `usr_users.require_password_change`, so an account sent here by that flag - one whose password was assigned by `/auth/sign-up` or `/auth/password-reset` rather than chosen - is done with it afterwards; this is the only endpoint that clears it. Note that access tokens issued before the change stay valid until they expire - this endpoint does not revoke them.

200.description: A JSON object confirming that the password was changed.

post.summary: Reset the password of an account
post.description: Replaces the password of the named account with a newly generated one, flags the account `require_password_change`, and mails the new password to the address on the row - the same mail `/auth/sign-up` sends, for the same reason. This is the endpoint for somebody who cannot sign in, so it takes no token and no current password: the only thing asked for is the username, and what protects the account is that the password goes to its stored address and is not in the response. No password is accepted from the caller either, or knowing a username would be enough to choose that account's password. An unknown username, a disabled account and an account without an address are all answered 200 exactly like a successful reset, having changed nothing, so the response cannot be used to find out which usernames exist. A mail that cannot be sent leaves the old password in force and answers 502, so nobody is locked out of a working account by a reset they asked for and never received. Note that access tokens issued before the reset stay valid until they expire - this endpoint does not revoke them, just as `/auth/password-change` does not. Throttled per client IP.

200.description: A JSON object confirming that the request was accepted. It does not say whether a mail went out, which would reveal whether the account exists.

get.description: Returns a newly generated password for the caller to adopt, of `length` characters (16-32, default 24). The bounds are those of `/auth/password-change`, so anything generated here is accepted there. `minuchars`, `minlchars`, `minnumbers` and `minschars` set how many upper case letters, lower case letters, digits and special characters the result must contain at least (defaults 3, 3, 3 and 3), and none of them may be set below its default, which is the policy floor. Their sum may not exceed `length`. The first and last characters are always a letter or a digit, never a special character. Every result is checked against the policy before it is returned. The password is generated per request and never stored, so it cannot be retrieved again - a caller that loses the response simply asks for another one. The response is marked `Cache-Control: no-store` to keep the secret out of proxy and browser caches.

200.description: A JSON object containing the generated password.

post.description: Creates a `usr_users` row for the given person at `ui_level` `pending` and mails them a generated password. No password is accepted from the caller: the account is given one that satisfies the policy and is flagged `require_password_change`, so it has to be replaced through `/auth/password-change` before the account is of any use. The generated password appears in the mail alone - it is not in the response, not logged, and cannot be retrieved afterwards, so an account whose mail never arrives has to be registered again. A username already taken or an email address already registered is refused with 409. A mail that cannot be sent rolls the account back and answers 502, so no account is ever left holding a password that was never delivered.

201.description: A JSON object confirming that the account was created.

post.summary: [admin] Register a new account on someone's behalf
post.description:
**Required scope:** `admin`

Creates an account exactly as `/auth/sign-up` does - same generated password, same `require_password_change`, same `pending` level and the same mail - and differs in two points. It requires a token carrying the `admin` scope, since the caller is registering somebody other than themselves. And it does not refuse an email address that is already registered to another account, so several accounts may share one address: registering on behalf of someone who has no address of their own is the case this exists for. The password still goes to that address, which means whoever owns it can read the credentials of every account registered against it - that is the trade this endpoint makes, and it is why it is behind `admin`. The username is still refused if it is taken, `usr_users.username` being unique.

201.description: A JSON object confirming that the account was created.

get.summary: [pending] Read the profile of the calling user
get.description:
**Required scope:** `pending`

Returns what the account the bearer token belongs to may know about itself: the `first_name`, `surname`, `email` and `img_avatar` that `PATCH /auth/me` writes, and beside them `username`, `uuid`, `ui_level`, `require_password_change` and the scopes the account holds. Those five are read-only here. This is the only way for an account to read its own row: `usr_users` is otherwise reachable through `/system-tables/users/read`, which requires the `admin` scope. `img_avatar` is sent on every call, so a response can be as large as the picture - it is base64 in the URL-safe alphabet and without `=` padding, which a client has to decode as such. The credential columns are never returned. Any bearer token of an enabled user is accepted, whatever its scopes, including an account still at `pending`.

200.description: A JSON object with the profile of the calling account, its identifiers, its interface level and the scopes it holds.

patch.summary: [pending] Change the profile of the calling user
patch.description:
**Required scope:** `pending`

Changes the profile of the account the bearer token belongs to: `first_name`, `surname`, `email` and `img_avatar`. Only the fields present in the request body are written - a field left out keeps its stored value, and a field sent as `null` is cleared, so one field can be changed without carrying the others along. A body that changes nothing is refused with 422. No other column of `usr_users` can be reached: `username`, `enable`, `ui_level` and the `token_scope_*` flags decide what an account may do and are changed through `/system-tables/users/update`, which requires the `admin` scope. An `email` already registered to another account is refused with 409. `img_avatar` travels as base64 and may not exceed 1048576 decoded bytes; its content is not inspected. Any bearer token of an enabled user is accepted, whatever its scopes, since maintaining one's own profile is not a privileged action - including an account still at `pending`.

200.description: A JSON object confirming that the profile was changed. The profile itself is not returned, so a request that changed a name is not answered with the whole avatar.

post.description:
**Required scope:** `read`

Search the translation vectors for the rows closest in meaning to `query`. The `query.language` value selects which vector table is searched (`tsl_embeddings_de`, `_fr`, `_it`, `_en`) and which translation column is returned as `text`; default is `de`. The `where` clause filters the rows of that vector table before the search. Hits come back in descending `similarity` (cosine, -1 to 1). Set `return_vectors` to also receive the query vector and each hit vector.

200.description: The matching rows in descending similarity, with the query echoed and total/count.

post.description:
**Required scope:** `read`

Search the translation texts for the rows whose wording best matches `query`, scored with BM25 by pg_search. The `query.language` value selects which search text table is searched (`tsl_search_texts_de`, `_fr`, `_it`, `_en`) and therefore which translation is returned as `text`; default is `de`. The `where` clause filters the rows of that table before the search. Hits come back in descending `bm25_score`, which is unbounded and only comparable within one result set. Matching is on terms, not on meaning, so a row sharing no term with `query` is not returned at all and `total` counts hits rather than candidates.

200.description: The matching rows in descending BM25 score, with the query echoed and total/count.

post.description:
**Required scope:** `read`

Search the translation texts for the rows matching `query`, with Postgres' own full text search: the text becomes a tsvector, the query becomes a tsquery through websearch_to_tsquery(), and the hits are ordered by ts_rank(). The `query.language` value selects which search text table is searched (`tsl_search_texts_de`, `_fr`, `_it`, `_en`) and which text search configuration (german, french, italian, english) stems both sides; default is `de`. The `where` clause filters the rows of that table before the search. `query` takes web search syntax: bare terms are ANDed, "quoted text" matches as a phrase, OR is available and a leading - excludes a term. Matching is on word stems, not on meaning, so a row sharing no stem with `query` is not returned at all and `total` counts hits rather than candidates.

200.description: The matching rows in descending rank, with the query echoed and total/count.

Query and stored text are stemmed by that same configuration, so one word form finds the others -- but matching stays lexical, not semantic: a word whose stem occurs in no row cannot match it. Input the parser cannot read is not an error, it is ignored. Must not be blank.

where.title: Where

total.title: Total
total.description: Number of rows matching both the query and `where`, before `limit` and `offset` are applied: how many hits the ranking has to offer, not how many were returned. Unlike a vector search this is not the candidate set -- a row whose text shares no stem with the query is not a weak hit but no hit at all, so `total` is usually far below `all`.

count.title: Count
count.description: Number of rows actually returned in `rows`, never more than `limit`.

all.title: All
all.description: Number of rows the language search text table offers to search at all, ignoring `where`: the pool `total` was narrowed down from. Rows without a stored search text are left out here too, since the search could never return them, so `all` equals `total` when `where` matches everything.

rows.title: Rows
rows.description: The matching rows, ordered by descending `rank`, so the best match comes first. None when nothing matched.

FullTextSearch.title: FullTextSearch
FullTextSearch.description: Full text search result set: echoes the query it was produced from and carries the matching rows, how many came back, how many matched in total, and how large the searchable pool is.

query.title: Query Text
query.description: Text to search for. It is turned into a tsquery by websearch_to_tsquery() in the language's text search configuration, so bare terms are ANDed, "quoted text" matches as a phrase, OR is available and a leading - excludes a term. Query and stored text are stemmed by that same configuration, so one word form finds the others -- but matching stays lexical, not semantic: a word whose stem occurs in no row cannot match it. Input the parser cannot read is not an error, it is ignored. Must not be blank.

where.title: Where
where.description: SQL WHERE clause, applied before the full text search runs, so it decides which rows are candidates at all. It can name columns of the language-specific search text table (tsl_search_texts_<language>) and of the joined tsl_translations row, with or without the table name in front. A bare `pk`, `created_at` or `updated_at` is the search text table's; the tsl_translations ones are `tsl_pk`, `tsl_created_at` and `tsl_updated_at`, or spell them out as `tsl_translations.pk` and so on. Every other tsl_translations column keeps its own name either way. Three of them are what scopes a search, because together they say where each translated text came from. `tsl_translations.fk_table` is the name of the source table whose attribute is translated -- a logical reference, not a database foreign key -- so `tsl_translations.fk_table = 'cur_curricula'` searches the curricula texts only, while `tsl_translations.fk_table IN ('prj_projects', 'cur_curricula')` and `tsl_translations.fk_table LIKE 'ops%'` widen that to several. `tsl_translations.fk_table_pk` is the primary key (pk) of the row in that source table, so `tsl_translations.fk_table = 'cur_curricula' AND tsl_translations.fk_table_pk = 5` narrows the search to the texts of one single curriculum; it is only meaningful together with `fk_table`, because every source table numbers its rows from 1 and `fk_table_pk = 5` on its own would match one unrelated row per table. `tsl_translations.fk_attribute` is the name of the attribute (column) in the source table whose text is translated, so `tsl_translations.fk_attribute = 'tsl_title'` searches titles and ignores descriptions. The three combine freely, as in `tsl_translations.fk_table = 'ops_operational_skills' AND tsl_translations.fk_attribute = 'tsl_description'`.

limit.title: Limit
limit.description: Maximum number of rows to return. Must be 1 or greater.

offset.title: Offset
offset.description: Number of rows to skip off the top of the ranking before `limit` is taken. ts_rank is deterministic for a given query and text, so paging is stable as long as the underlying rows do not change.

language.title: Language
language.description: Language used for translated fields. It selects both which search text table is searched and which Postgres text search configuration (german, french, italian, english) stems the stored text and the query.

LogEntry.title: LogEntry
LogEntry.description:
Append-only audit trail of all data changes in the `skills` schema.

One row is written for every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the audited base
tables by the generic ``skills.log_change()`` trigger (defined in
``pg_migrations/skills/pg_db_cmd.py::get_sql_logging_trigger``). Each entry

it happened, and the full row state before and/or after the change as JSONB.

The trigger fires AFTER the row operation, so ``new_val`` reflects the final
persisted row (including the ``updated_at`` set by the BEFORE-UPDATE
``set_updated_at()`` trigger).

Idea: https://www.cybertec-postgresql.com/en/tracking-changes-in-postgresql/

LogEntrySystem.title: LogEntrySystem
LogEntrySystem.description:
Append-only audit trail of all data changes in the `system` schema.

One row is written for every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the audited base
tables (``usr_users``, ``org_organizations``, ``usr_2_org`` — see
``TRIGGER_TABLES``) by the generic ``system.log_change()`` trigger (defined in
``pg_migrations/system/pg_db_cmd.py::get_sql_logging_trigger``). Each entry
captures which table and row changed, the kind of change, who made it, when
it happened, and the full row state before and/or after the change as JSONB.

The trigger fires AFTER the row operation, so ``new_val`` reflects the final
persisted row (including the ``updated_at`` set by the BEFORE-UPDATE
``set_updated_at()`` trigger).

Rows are only ever inserted — the application never updates or deletes them,
which is why this is the one table in the schema without an ``updated_at``.

Idea: https://www.cybertec-postgresql.com/en/tracking-changes-in-postgresql/

current_password.title: Current password
current_password.description: The password in force right now, re-checked here even though the request is already authenticated: a stolen token alone must not be enough to lock the owner out of their own account.

new_password.title: New password
new_password.description: The password to set. Only a length bound is enforced - no composition rules, which push users towards predictable substitutions rather than longer secrets.

PasswordChange.title: PasswordChange
PasswordChange.description:
Request body of /auth/password-change: the caller's current password and the one to replace
it with. The username is deliberately absent - it is taken from the bearer token, so the
endpoint can only ever change the password of the account that is calling it.

changed.title: Password changed
changed.description: Always true. Present so the response is a self-describing JSON object rather than an empty body. Also means `require_password_change` is now false for this account.

PasswordChangeResult.title: PasswordChangeResult

username.title: Username
username.description: Login name to check. An unknown name is answered like a wrong password, so the response cannot be used to find out which usernames exist.

password.title: Password
password.description: Plain-text password, verified against the Argon2id hash stored for the user.

PasswordCheck.title: PasswordCheck
PasswordCheck.description:
Request body of /auth/password-check: the one credential pair to verify. A body rather than
query parameters, so the password does not end up in a URL, a proxy log or a browser history.

valid.title: Credentials valid
valid.description: True only when the username exists, the password matches and the account is enabled. False in every other case, without saying which of the three failed.

ui_level.title: UI level
ui_level.description: The `usr_users.ui_level` of the checked account: the interface level it is meant to be presented at, so a caller can pick the interface in the same round trip it verifies the credentials in. `none` whenever `valid` is false, and also whenever the account itself has no level set. Presentation only - it grants nothing, and what a token may do is decided by the `token_scope_*` columns alone.

require_password_change.title: Password change required
require_password_change.description: True when the account has to replace its password, and the caller is not doing so. False when the account does not have to replace its password, or the caller is doing so. Presentation only - it grants nothing, and what a token may do is decided by the `token_scope_*` columns alone.

PasswordCheckResult.title: PasswordCheckResult
PasswordCheckResult.description:
Response body of /auth/password-check: the verdict on one credential pair, plus the interface
level the account is meant to be shown. Still no token and no user record, and a rejected check
gives no hint as to which part was wrong - `ui_level` reads `none` there, which is also what a
row that has no level set carries, so the two cannot be told apart.

password.title: Generated password
password.description: A freshly generated password of the requested length, drawn from Python's `secrets` module by cacao-password-generator, mixing upper case, lower case, digits and punctuation. A different value on every call.

PasswordGenerated.title: PasswordGenerated
PasswordGenerated.description:
Response body of /auth/password-generator: a suggested password and nothing else. It is not
stored, not remembered and not tied to any account - it only becomes a password once the caller
passes it to /auth/password-change.

username.title: Username
username.description: Login name of the account to reset. An unknown name is answered exactly like a known one, so the response cannot be used to find out which usernames exist.

PasswordReset.title: PasswordReset
PasswordReset.description:
Request body of /auth/password-reset: the account whose password is to be replaced. Named by
`username` rather than by email because `usr_users.username` is unique while `usr_users.email` is
not - several accounts may share one address, so an address does not identify an account to reset.

No password field, and deliberately no proof of anything: this is the endpoint for somebody who
cannot log in, so the only thing it can ask for is the name of the account. What protects the
account is that the new password goes to the address on the row and nowhere else.

accepted.title: Reset accepted
accepted.description: Always true. Present so the response is a self-describing JSON object rather than an empty body. It is not a confirmation that a mail went out: an unknown username, a disabled account and an account without an email address are all answered this way, having changed nothing.

PasswordResetResult.title: PasswordResetResult
PasswordResetResult.description:
Response body of /auth/password-reset. `accepted` says the request was understood and acted on
as far as it could be - not that a password was mailed, which is a thing the caller is deliberately
not told, since it would reveal whether the account exists.

where.title: Where
where.description: SQL WHERE clause, applied before the full text search runs, so it decides which rows are candidates at all. It can name columns of the language-specific search text table (tsl_search_texts_<language>) and of the joined tsl_translations row, with or without the table name in front. A bare `pk`, `created_at` or `updated_at` is the search text table's; the tsl_translations ones are `tsl_pk`, `tsl_created_at` and `tsl_updated_at`, or spell them out as `tsl_translations.pk` and so on. Every other tsl_translations column keeps its own name either way. || Three of them are what scopes a search, because together they say where each translated text came from. `tsl_translations.fk_table` is the name of the source table whose attribute is translated -- a logical reference, not a database foreign key -- so `tsl_translations.fk_table = 'cur_curricula'` searches the curricula texts only, and `tsl_translations.fk_table IN ('prj_projects', 'cur_curricula')` or `tsl_translations.fk_table LIKE 'ops%'` widen that to several. || `tsl_translations.fk_table_pk` is the primary key (pk) of the row in that source table, so `tsl_translations.fk_table = 'cur_curricula' AND tsl_translations.fk_table_pk = 5` narrows the search to the texts of one single curriculum. It is only meaningful together with `fk_table`: every source table numbers its rows from 1, so `fk_table_pk = 5` on its own matches one unrelated row per table. || `tsl_translations.fk_attribute` is the name of the attribute (column) in the source table whose text is translated, so `tsl_translations.fk_attribute = 'tsl_title'` searches titles and ignores descriptions. || The three combine freely, e.g. `tsl_translations.fk_table = 'ops_operational_skills' AND tsl_translations.fk_attribute = 'tsl_description'`.

offset.title: Offset
offset.description: Number of rows to skip off the top of the ranking before `limit` is taken. Note that the ranking is recomputed per request from a freshly embedded query, and two embeddings of the same text are not bit-identical, so rows with near-equal scores can change places between pages.

rerank_result.title: Rerank Result

The vector search selects the rows first (so `limit` still decides how many are considered), then the rerank model scores the query against each row text and the rows come back in that order, each carrying its `rerank_similarity`. where.title: Where
where.description:
SQL WHERE clause selecting which branches of the hierarchy are returned. Any table of the hierarchy may be filtered on, not only prj_projects: cur_curricula, cur_type_degree, aoe_2_cur, aoe_area_of_operational_expertises, ops_2_aoe_2_cur, ops_operational_skills, ops_uses, ops_levels, pec_2_ops_2_aoe_2_cur, pec_performance_criteria, pec_learning_locations and pec_levels. Every column must be qualified with its table name - an unqualified name is ambiguous across the hierarchy and is rejected. Conditions combine with AND, OR and NOT, may be grouped with parentheses, and use the usual SQL operators. A condition on a deeper table prunes the whole tree to the branches satisfying it: filtering on a curriculum returns only the projects holding it, and only that curriculum inside them. Two limits apply. The translated *_txt fields are resolved from tsl_translations at read time and are not columns, so filter the stored tsl_* key instead. And statement keywords (SELECT, DELETE, CREATE, ...) are stripped from the clause before it is used, including inside quoted literals, so a string value containing one of them is silently altered. Examples:
- `prj_projects.pk = 1` - one project with everything below it
- `prj_projects.pk = 1 AND cur_curricula.pk = 32` - a single curriculum of that project
- `prj_projects.pk = 1 AND (cur_curricula.pk = 30 OR cur_curricula.pk = 32)` - two of them
- `cur_curricula.pk IN (30, 32)` - the same, with the project derived from the curricula
- `aoe_area_of_operational_expertises.pk = 342` - every branch leading to that area
- `cur_curricula.pk = 32 AND ops_operational_skills.tsl_title IS NOT NULL` - levels combined
- `prj_projects.pk = 1 AND cur_curricula.created_at > '2020-01-01'` - non-key columns

TokenSystem.title: TokenSystem
TokenSystem.description:
The bearer tokens a user may present — the record every request is checked against.

A signed JWT proves on its own that it was minted by this application and is
not yet expired, which is precisely the problem: nothing about it can be taken
back before ``exp`` passes. This table is what makes that possible.
``auth_service.get_current_user`` looks up every presented token here after
validating its signature, and refuses it unless a row matches and that row is
enabled — so the row, not the signature, decides whether a token is still
current. ``type`` records which of the three channels of ``UsrTokenType`` the
token was issued for — ``ui``, ``api`` or ``mcp`` — mirroring the per-channel
credential columns on ``usr_users``. It is more than a label:
``auth_service.create_access_token`` gives a ``ui`` token the fixed
``UI_ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL`` instead of the account's ``access_token_ttl``, because
the interface has no way to refresh one.

A user may hold several tokens, one per row. Only the SHA-256 digest of a
token is kept, in ``token_hash`` — verification hashes what the client
presented and looks that digest up, so resolving a token stays a single
indexed query while the token itself never reaches the database, its indexes
or ``log_entries``. The digest is deliberately unsalted and deliberately not
run through the Argon2id hasher used for ``usr_users.password_hash``: a token
is generated with 256 bits of entropy, so hashing speed buys an attacker
nothing, whereas a per-row salt would force a scan over every row to find a
match and a slow KDF would be paid on every single request. The price is that
a token can be shown only once, when it is issued: nothing on the row can be
read back to reconstruct it, and nothing on it makes one token recognisable
from another afterwards either. ``token_scope`` is meant to say what a token was
issued for, but is reserved — no code path writes it yet.

Only tokens whose ``enable`` flag is true are accepted, which makes revoking
a token a single UPDATE instead of a DELETE and leaves the row in place for
auditing. ``fk_user`` cascades, so deleting a user removes every token issued
to it.

UserChange.title: UserChange
UserChange.description:
Request body of PATCH /auth/me: the profile fields to change, every one of them optional. What is
written is decided by which keys the body actually carries, not by which values are non-null - a
field left out of the body keeps its stored value, and a field sent as `null` clears it. The
distinction is what makes changing one field possible: `img_avatar` is a picture held in the row
itself, so a caller correcting the spelling of a name must neither have to send the picture along
nor lose it by leaving it out.

An ApiBase rather than a plain BaseModel, for `img_avatar` alone: JSON has no byte type, so the
field travels as base64, and without that configured on the request side the base64 text itself
would be stored as the picture.

The username is deliberately absent, as it is on PasswordChange - the account is taken from the
bearer token, so the endpoint can only ever change the profile of the account calling it. So is
every other column of `usr_users`: `enable`, `ui_level` and the `token_scope_*` flags decide what
an account may do and are nobody's own business to set, and `username` is the name every token is
issued against. Those go through `/system-tables/users/update`, which requires the `admin` scope.

an HTTP error, never `changed: false`. The profile is deliberately not echoed back - `img_avatar`
would put the whole picture into the answer to a request that changed a name. A caller that wants
the stored state reads GET /auth/me.

surname.title: Surname

img_avatar.title: Avatar

UserInfo.title: UserInfo

Response body of GET /auth/me: what the calling account may know about itself. The four fields
PATCH /auth/me writes, and beside them the read-only ones a client would otherwise have no way to
reach - `usr_users` can only be read through `/system-tables/users/read`, which requires the

UserSystem.title: UserSystem
UserSystem.description:
A user account — and the row that decides what any token issued to it may carry.

A row can only be used to log in when ``enable`` is true and both ``username``
and ``password_hash`` are set — all three are checked by
``app/authentication/auth_service.py``. The ``token_scope_*`` columns decide
which scopes an issued access token may carry, one boolean per scope, so an
account is granted exactly the set it needs rather than the nearest rung of a
fixed ladder of roles. ``ui_level`` is the one place a rung is still named, and
it is a presentation level only — it grants nothing.

The row carries one set of credentials per channel a token can be issued for,
the three members of ``UsrTokenType``. The unprefixed columns (``username`` /
``password_hash`` / ``access_token_ttl`` / ``token_scope_*``) are the set every
login goes through today, for the ``ui`` and the ``api`` channel alike. The
``api_`` and ``mcp_`` prefixed columns repeat that same set for a programmatic
REST client and for the MCP server, which is a separate application; they are
columns of their own so a channel can be renamed, re-secreted, given its own
token lifetime or locked out without touching the others. Both are reserved —
no code path in this API reads them yet. The seed writes the ``mcp_`` set as a
copy of the unprefixed one, so an account already reaches the MCP server with
the same credentials, while the ``api_`` set is left unset.

The credential columns (``password_hash``, ``otp_hash``, ``api_password_hash``,
``mcp_password_hash``) are deliberately excluded from the API model in
``app/api/system_tables/usr_users/models.py``, so they can neither be read back
nor written through the CRUD endpoints.

Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on this table is captured in ``log_entries``
by the ``system.log_change()`` trigger.

A user may belong to several organizations and an organization may have many

UsrTokenType.title: UsrTokenType
UsrTokenType.description:
Channel a ``usr_tokens`` row was issued for.

One member per set of credentials on ``usr_users``: ``ui`` for the user
interface and ``api`` for a programmatic REST client, which both authenticate
through the unprefixed columns today, and ``mcp`` for the MCP server, which has
the ``mcp_`` prefixed set of its own. More than a label — ``ui`` is what makes
``auth_service.create_access_token`` override the account's lifetime with
``UI_ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL``. Persisted as the lowercase member *value* in a native
PostgreSQL enum type named ``usrtokentype``. A member added here reaches the
database only through ``make migrate`` in ``pg_migrations/system/``, since
Alembic writes no DDL for it — until then the column rejects the new label.

UsrTokenType: ui=UI, api=API, mcp=MCP

UsrUiLevelType.title: UsrUiLevelType
UsrUiLevelType.description:
Level of the user interface a ``usr_users`` row is presented at.

The members from ``PUBLIC`` on are named after ``auth_service.Scope`` and kept
in its order, least privileged first, so a level reads the same way as the
scope of the same name. ``NONE`` and ``PENDING`` are the two that name no
scope and so correspond to nothing a token can carry: ``NONE`` sits below
every level and is the default, ``PENDING`` just above it, for an account that
exists but whose level has not been decided yet.

Unlike the ``token_scope_*`` columns, which are an independent boolean each, a
level is a single rung: it says which interface an account is meant to be
shown, never what it is allowed to do. Persisted as the lowercase member
*value* in a native PostgreSQL enum type named ``usruileveltype`` (see
``db_common.enum_column``). A member added here reaches the database only
through ``make migrate`` in ``pg_migrations/system/``, since Alembic writes no
DDL for it — until then the column rejects the new label.
